idiom_name: circe Encoder.forProductN / narrowed derived encoder; narrow case-class DTO
implementation_notes: In the circe stack the projection is an explicit Encoder: Encoder.forProduct3("id", "reference", "total")(o => (o.id, o.reference, o.total)) emits exactly those keys, and a derived encoder can be narrowed after the fact with deriveEncoder[Order].mapJsonObject(_.filter { case (k, _) => keep(k) }) or .remove("field"). The safer alternative in a codebase is a separate narrow case class with its own derived encoder, because the wire contract then exists as a type rather than as a lambda. What replaces the classic filter object is the Encoder instance; filtering a JsonObject by hand (mapObject/filterKeys) is still justified when the key set is supplied per request at runtime, and for Kafka/streaming pipelines the same encoder serves as the boundary where the projection happens.
pitfalls: Automatic derivation serializes every case-class field: adding a field to the domain model silently widens every receiver's contract unless the encoder is written explicitly (which is why semi-automatic derivation is the safer default here).
mapJsonObject copies the whole JsonObject per message; that is fine at moderate volume but visible in high-throughput streams, where a flat DTO encoder avoids the intermediate tree.
caseClass.copy(...) keeps all fields and is therefore not a projection - reaching for copy() to build a view produces a JSON payload with the internal fields still present but stale.

Jackson-based Scala stacks behave differently from circe (annotations on the class instead of encoder instances), so mixing both in one service gives two incompatible notions of the same wire contract.
